title: Open Graph images that match the article
metaTitle: Open Graph images that match the piece
excerpt: A chat preview should be readable at a glance and carry the article's point. A wordless hero crop often fails. A poster of keywords fails too.

faqs.question: What should an Open Graph image show?
faqs.answer: It should be readable at a glance in a chat and carry the point of that article. A short line and a calm image beat a crop of the hero with no words, and they also beat a poster stuffed with keywords. If the line is not true of the article, change the line or change the image.

faqs.question: Can I reuse the hero photograph as the share image?
faqs.answer: Only when the photograph still makes sense as a small rectangle with no surrounding article. Many heroes rely on the headline beside them. Once the headline is gone, the crop is a nice picture that does not say which piece this is. Add a few words, or choose a frame that already contains the point.

faqs.question: Should every article have its own image?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the articles make different claims. A single studio logo on every share teaches people nothing about the piece and makes a row of links look automated. A template is fine. A template that never changes its words is a logo with extra steps.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Open Graph image design is the layout of the picture a chat shows when someone pastes your article. It should be readable at a glance and carry that article's point. A crop of the hero with no words often fails. A poster of keywords fails too.

The person seeing it has not opened the piece. They are in a thread, on a phone, deciding whether your link is the one to tap. The image has about as much time as a book cover on a crowded table.

## A chat is a different surface

The article page can be quiet. Large type, a photograph, a first paragraph that states the answer. The share card cannot borrow that layout. It is a wide rectangle, often cropped again by the app, sitting beside a domain name and a line of title. If the point of the article only exists in the body, the card is a shrug.

Design the card as its own frame. Ask what a colleague would need in order to forward it without adding a paragraph of explanation. Usually that is the subject and the decision, not the mood. "One official URL" is a point. A photograph of mountains, with no words, is a mood. Mood can support the point. It cannot replace it when ten other links in the same thread also have pleasant photographs.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether you would share the page with a friend, and whether the heading is a fair summary rather than a shock. The share image is that question made visible. If you would be embarrassed to drop the card into a founder's chat, it is not done. If the card only makes sense to someone who already read the piece, it is not doing the job of a preview.

Google's title systems also read `og:title` as one of the sources they may use when they build a title link. The Open Graph title is not a dumping ground for a second, stuffed headline. Write it as a clear name for the page, in the same language as the article. The image and the title should agree. A card that says one thing and a title tag that says another is two brands in one paste.

## Readable at a glance

Hold the design at the size of a thumbnail before you fall in love with it at the size of a poster. If you cannot read the line, the line is decoration. If the line wraps into four lines, it is a paragraph, and paragraphs do not survive a chat.

Use a short line. Six to ten words is enough for most studio articles. Set it in the type the brand already uses, at a size that would still work if the app crops the edges. Keep the contrast obvious. A pale gray sentence on a pale photograph looks refined on a calibrated monitor and disappears on a phone in daylight.

Leave room. A card that is full to the edges will lose the last word to a rounded mask or a play button. Put the line in a region you are willing to bet will remain visible. Test the file in an actual chat, not only in a generator's preview. Slack, iMessage, LinkedIn, and a private Discord do not crop the same way. You do not have to please all of them perfectly. You do have to look at two.

The photograph under the type still has to be a photograph of something. Hanabi's public visual habit is specific and calm: a place, an object, a desk, a product. Wabisabi's world is tactile. Thomas Bewick's is editorial and heritage. The card can share that restraint. It should not become a collage of logos, arrows, and three competing slogans.

## Why a wordless hero crop fails

The hero on the article is allowed to be quiet because the headline sits next to it. Take the headline away and many heroes become anonymous. A beach at sunrise is lovely. It does not tell a founder whether this link is about meta descriptions, canonicals, or a case study. In a thread of five links, the anonymous ones get skipped, or they get opened by accident and closed.

A crop also lies when the hero's subject is off-center. The page shows a full desk. The card shows a mug and a corner of a laptop. The mug was never the point. You have published a different picture than the one the article argued with.

If you love the photograph, keep it, and add the smallest amount of type that restores the point. The type should say the decision, not the category. "Keep one official URL" is a decision. "SEO tips" is a category. Categories are how a studio starts to look like a content mill even when the article underneath is careful.

There is a second failure mode. The hero is a portrait, a product, or a screenshot with tiny UI text. Shrunk into a card, the UI text becomes noise, and the portrait becomes a face with no name. Either add a line the card can own, or choose a different frame for sharing. The article can keep its hero. The card does not have to be a literal excerpt of the same pixels.

## Why a keyword poster fails

The other temptation is a slide. Bold phrase, second bold phrase, a row of tools, the studio logo the size of a billboard. It is readable. It is also an ad, and it often repeats the title in louder type. The reader has the title next to the image already. The image that shouts the title again is the visual version of a stuffed snippet.

Keyword posters age badly. They lock the article to a phrase you may want to stop repeating. They make every piece look like the same template with the noun swapped, which is the pattern founders have learned to distrust. And they tend to promise a completeness the article should be too honest to claim. "The complete guide" on a card is a lot to live up to in the first paragraph.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) rejects keyword stuffing and boilerplate that makes pages indistinguishable. A series of share images that differ only by a swapped phrase is the same mistake in pictures. A few true words help. A pile of synonyms does not. If the card would look spammy as a title, it will look spammy as an image.

Brand still belongs there, quietly. A small wordmark or a consistent color is how a person recognizes the studio across a month of links. It should not be the message. The message is the article's point. The brand is the signature.

## A template that can change its mind

Build one template, not one image. A fixed frame, a place for a photograph, a place for one line, and a small mark. Then change the photograph and the line per article. That is how a series looks related without looking automated.

Hanabi designs this kind of frame in Figma, next to the rest of the brand system, and builds the site in Next.js so the page can point at the right file. The file should be a real image with a stable URL, not a screenshot someone pasted into a doc and re-exported at the wrong size. When the line changes, export a new file or version the path. An immutable cache will keep serving the old card long after you "updated" it, which is the same lesson as any other asset: changed bytes need a new key.

Write the line the way you write the description. Outcome or decision, not a tease. "Update the post when the answer changes." "Show the invoice, not a tour." "A feed is a follow without an account." Those lines are useful even if the person never clicks. A tease ("You won't believe this crawl budget trick") fails the people-first test and sounds nothing like a careful studio.

Keep a folder of the cards beside the drafts. When you retitle an article, update the card in the same pass. A card that still carries the working title is a public correction waiting to happen. So is a card with a claim you later softened in the text. The image will travel farther than the paragraph, and it will not update itself when you edit the essay.

## What to leave off

Leave off the publication date unless the date is the point, and even then check that you will update the image when you update the date. A card that says "2022" on a page you revised this year is an obsolete title in picture form. Google calls out titles that keep an old year while the visible heading has moved on. The share image has the same rot, and more people see it.

Leave off prices, headcount, awards, and client quotes you would not put in the article. A card is not a place to invent a metric. Leave off a screenshot of a dashboard with real customer data. Leave off a stock-looking collage of handshakes. If the photograph needs a credit, the article caption can carry it. The card is too small for a credit line and a headline and a logo.

Leave off the entire navigation of the website, shrunk to unreadability. A miniature homepage is not a summary. It is a reduction. Summaries use words.

If the article is one of a series, you may put the series name in small type. Do not let the series name replace the point. "Studio notes, issue 40" tells a subscriber where they are. It tells a stranger nothing. The stranger is the person the card is for.

## Check the card the way the article is checked

Before you publish, paste the URL into a channel you actually use. Look at it on a phone. Ask a teammate what they think the article is about, without letting them open it. If they name the point, ship it. If they name the mood, or the keyword, rewrite the line.

Then open the article and see whether the card told the truth. The first paragraph should cash the promise. A card that oversells is worse than a quiet one, because it spends trust the page then has to earn back. [An intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) is the right next step when you want a second pair of eyes on the system: the frame, the type, and the kinds of lines your articles should be allowed to wear.

The card gets someone to the piece once. A feed is how they hear about the next one without waiting to be tagged. [RSS and why a studio should keep it](/blog/rss-and-why-a-studio-should-keep-it) is the next piece, because a share image is a single introduction, and a feed is the ongoing promise that the writing continues.
